Always check the ﬁlm: Retained central venous catheter
fragment in a patient with intestinal failure

A 7‐year‐old male with a history of intestinal failure due to
intestinal atresia dependent on parenteral nutrition via
central venous catheter (CVC) presented to an outside
institution for replacement of existing CVC due to
thrombosis. Operative reports described the placement
of a left internal jugular (IJ) 6.6‐French single‐lumen‐
tunneled CVC and removal of the existing right IJ‐
tunneled CVC. The report stated that the tip of the new
CVC was conﬁrmed to be located at the cavoatrial
junction via ﬂuoroscopy. A radiographic image was not
available for our review and the ﬂuoroscopic image was
not read by a radiologist. Our institutional protocol
recommends obtaining a chest radiograph to evaluate
the CVC tip location every 1 year for children under 2
years of age, every 2 years for children over age
2 years, or following CVC placement/replacement. The
chest radiograph obtained (Figure 1) noted the new
left IJ CVC but also a large retained fragment of the prior
right IJ CVC. The retained CVC fragment was then
removed by an interventional radiologist by snare via
the right common femoral vein access. There were no
complications.

Mechanical issues, including fracture, are common
complications of CVCs.1 Speciﬁcally, retained CVC
fragments
after
attempted
removal
have
been
described in the literature in pediatric patients with
prolonged use of CVCs, with incidence ranging from
0.3% to 2%.2–4 Ongoing radiographic surveillance is
recommended
to
assess
the
central
location
by
ensuring the catheter tip resides at or near the
cavoatrial junction.5 Clinicians caring for children with
CVCs should familiarize themselves with the radio-
graphic appearance of normally placed CVCs. Person-
ally reviewing images, and avoiding relying only on
operative, ﬂuoroscopic, or radiology reports, to ensure
the central location or integrity of the catheter can
maximize the safety of long‐term CVC use in this high‐
risk group.
